analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans that cover prescription drugs to cover prescription contraceptives equally.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 35 Senate cosponsors from both parties and a Senate hearing, but never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred group and individual health plans from excluding prescription contraceptive drugs, devices, and related outpatient services when the plan already covers other prescription drugs and outpatient services. It also would have forbidden insurers from denying enrollment over contraceptive use, paying individuals to accept weaker coverage, or rewarding doctors for withholding contraception. Plans could still apply normal deductibles and copays, but no higher for contraception than for other drugs and services.
analysis.who_benefits: Women of reproductive age with private health insurance, who the bill's findings say spend 68 percent more than men on out-of-pocket health care costs, largely because contraceptives are typically excluded from plans that otherwise cover prescription drugs. Their families also benefit from better ability to plan and space pregnancies, which the bill's findings link to lower infant mortality and fewer unintended pregnancies.

how_it_helps.text: Plans that cover other outpatient prescription drugs and devices could no longer exclude FDA-approved prescription contraceptive drugs, devices, and generic equivalents [S3].
Plans that cover other outpatient services could no longer exclude contraceptive services such as consultations, examinations, and procedures, including natural family planning [S3].

Insurers could not deny or end enrollment because of a person's use or potential use of contraception, pay individuals to accept weaker protections, or penalize doctors for prescribing contraception [S3].
Cost-sharing for contraception could be imposed but capped at what the plan charges for comparable drugs and services, preventing insurers from dodging the rule with extra fees [S3].

The bill's findings cite roughly 3.6 million unintended pregnancies a year, about 60 percent of all pregnancies, and studies showing each dollar spent on family planning saves $4 to $14 in pregnancy and health care costs [S3].
The same rules would have applied to coverage sold in the individual market, not just employer plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor plans, who would cover contraceptives they had often excluded. The bill's findings argue this is cost-effective because preventing unintended pregnancy is cheaper than paying for pregnancy-related care, but premiums could rise modestly for all enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Mandated coverage adds to insurers' and employers' benefit costs, and critics of benefit mandates argue those costs can be passed to all enrollees through higher premiums or absorbed by reduced wages [S3].

The requirement is an equity standard, not a free benefit: plans that cover no other prescription drugs or outpatient services would owe no contraceptive coverage, and normal deductibles and copays still apply [S3].
Some people object on religious or moral grounds to being required to obtain or pay for contraceptive coverage through insurance; the bill as written contained no conscience exemption [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits reach a large population: most women of childbearing age rely on private employment-related insurance, and the bill's findings say contraceptive coverage reduces unintended pregnancy, abortion, and infant mortality while saving public money. The main cost is a modest increase in premiums shared broadly across enrollees, which the findings suggest is offset by avoided pregnancy-related costs. The lack of any conscience exemption is a genuine design gap, and the equity standard leaves plans with no drug coverage untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee that received the bill held a hearing on it in July 1998 but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on May 20, 1997, joined by eight original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats Harry Reid, Barbara Mikulski, Richard Durbin, Patty Murray, and Republicans John Warner, John Chafee, Susan Collins, and James Jeffords [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which had jurisdiction over health benefits [S5].
Ultimately 35 senators cosponsored the bill, 28 Democrats and 7 Republicans [S4].
The committee held a hearing on July 21, 1998, with the proceedings printed as S.Hrg. 105-604, but no markup or floor vote followed [S5].
No further action was taken before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers kept the ability to exclude prescription contraceptives from otherwise comprehensive drug coverage, saving on benefit costs for one more Congress. The women paying full out-of-pocket prices for contraception got nothing from the bill's death; a nearly identical equity standard was not enacted at the federal level during this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: a Republican senator sponsored the bill and 35 cosponsors split 28 Democrats and 7 Republicans, though no vote was ever taken to test that support.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the common practice of covering prescription drugs generally while excluding prescription contraceptives, forcing insurers to pay for benefits they had long priced out of plans. The savings from those exclusions came out of the pockets of insured women.
Employers would bear somewhat richer benefit packages and potentially higher premiums, but the equity rule also protected employees and could reduce costs from unintended pregnancies.
Insurance coverage of prescription contraceptives would expand the number of patients able to afford these products, with cost-sharing capped at the plan's normal drug cost-sharing.
